entries.b83de0cfcd9db4b32809ffe8bd9cc3167a0e80e0: <div sID="gen6105" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="2Sam.8" sID="2Sam.8"/> <div eID="gen6105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6106" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6107" type="x-p"/> David having sought first the kingdom of God and the righteousness thereof, settling the ark as soon as he was himself well settled, we are here told how all other things were added to him. Here is an account, I. Of his conquests. He triumphed, 1. Over the Philistines, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.1">ver. 1</reference>. 2. Over the Moabites, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">ver. 2</reference>. 3. Over the king of Zobah, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3-2Sam.8.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. 4. Over the Syrians, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.5-2Sam.8.8">ver. 5-8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.13">13</reference>. 5. Over the Edomites, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.14">ver. 14</reference>. II. Of the presents that were brought him and the wealth he got from the nations he subdued, which he dedicated to God, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.9-2Sam.8.12">ver. 9-12</reference>. III. Of his court, the administration of his government (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.15">ver. 15</reference>), and his chief officers, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.16-2Sam.8.18">ver. 16-18</reference>. This gives us a general idea of the prosperity of David's reign.
entries.f6d736d470d436d1d1190ab4f95f3f58ab372ac0: <div eID="gen6107" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6106" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Conquests. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1042.)</title> <div sID="gen6108" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And after this it came to pass, that David smote the Philistines, and subdued them: and David took Metheg-ammah out of the hand of the Philistines. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he smote Moab, and measured them with a line, casting them down to the ground; even with two lines measured he to put to death, and with one full line to keep alive. And <hi type="italic">so</hi> the Moabites became David's servants, <hi type="italic">and</hi> brought gifts. <hi type="super">3</hi> David smote also Hadadezer, the son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as he went to recover his border at the river Euphrates. <hi type="super">4</hi> And David took from him a thousand <hi type="italic">chariots,</hi> and seven hundred horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen: and David houghed all the chariot <hi type="italic">horses,</hi> but reserved of them <hi type="italic">for</hi> a hundred chariots. <hi type="super">5</hi> And when the Syrians of Damascus came to succour Hadadezer king of Zobah, David slew of the Syrians two and twenty thousand men. <hi type="super">6</hi> Then David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus: and the Syrians became servants to David, <hi type="italic">and</hi> brought gifts. And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> preserved David whithersoever he went. <hi type="super">7</hi> And David took the shields of gold that were on the servants of Hadadezer, and brought them to Jerusalem. <hi type="super">8</hi> And from Betah, and from Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, king David took exceeding much brass. <div eID="gen6108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6109" type="x-p"/> God had given David rest from all his enemies that opposed him and made head against him; and he having made a good use of that rest, has now commission given him to make war upon them, and to act offensively for the avenging of Israel's quarrels and the recovery of their rights; for as yet they were not in full possession of that country to which by the promise of God they were entitled. <div eID="gen6109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6110" type="x-p"/> I. He quite subdued the Philistines, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.1">v. 1</reference>. They had attacked him when they thought him weak (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.17">ch. v. 17</reference>), and went by the worst then; but, when he found himself strong, he attacked them, and made himself master of their country. They had long been vexatious and oppressive to Israel. Saul got no ground against them; but David completed Israel's deliverance out of their hands, which Samson had begun long before, <reference osisRef="Judg.13.5">Judg. xiii. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Metheg-ammah</hi> was <hi type="italic">Gath</hi> (the chief and royal city of the Philistines) and the towns belonging to it, among which there was a constant garrison kept by the Philistines on the hill Ammah (<reference osisRef="2Sam.2.24">2 Sam. ii. 24</reference>), which was <hi type="italic">Metheg,</hi> a <hi type="italic">bridle</hi> (so it signifies) or <hi type="italic">curb</hi> upon the people of Israel; this David took out of their hand and used it as a curb upon them. Thus, when the strong man is disarmed, the armour wherein he trusted is taken from him, and used against him, <reference osisRef="Luke.11.22">Luke xi. 22</reference>. And after the long and frequent struggles which the saints have had with the powers of darkness, like Israel with the Philistines, the Son of David shall tread them all under their feet and make the saints more than conquerors. <div eID="gen6110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6111" type="x-p"/> II. He smote the Moabites, and made them tributaries to Israel, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">v. 2</reference>. He divided the country into three parts, two of which he destroyed, casting down the strong-holds, and putting all to the sword; the third part he spared, to till the ground and be servants to Israel. Dr. Lightfoot says, "He laid them on the ground and measured them with a cord, who should be slain and who should live;" and this is called <hi type="italic">meting out the valley of Succoth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.60.6">Ps. lx. 6</reference>. The Jews say he used this severity with the Moabites because they had slain his parents and brethren, whom he put under the protection of the king of Moab during his exile, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.3-1Sam.22.4">1 Sam. xxii. 3, 4</reference>. He did it in justice, because they had been dangerous enemies to the Israel of God; and in policy, because, if left in their strength, they still would have been so. But observe, Though it was necessary that two-thirds should be cut off, yet the line that was to keep alive, though it was but one, is ordered to be a full line. Be sure to give that length enough; let the line of mercy be stretched to the utmost <hi type="italic">in favorem vitæ—so as to favour life.</hi> Acts of indemnity must be construed so as to enlarge the favour. Now Balaam's prophecy was fulfilled, <hi type="italic">A sceptre shall arise out of Israel, and shall smite the corners of Moab,</hi> to the utmost of which the fatal line extended, <reference osisRef="Num.24.17">Num. xxiv. 17</reference>. The Moabites continued tributaries to Israel till after the death of Ahab, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.4-2Kgs.3.5">2 Kings iii. 4, 5</reference>. Then they rebelled and were never reduced. <div eID="gen6111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6112" type="x-p"/> III. He smote the Syrians or Aramites. Of them there were two distinct kingdoms, as we find them spoken of in the title of the <reference osisRef="Ps.60.1-Ps.60.12">60th Psalm</reference>: <hi type="italic">Aram Naharaim,—Syria of the rivers,</hi> whose head city was Damascus (famed for its rivers, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.12">2 Kings v. 12</reference>), and <hi type="italic">Aram Zobah,</hi> which joined to it, but extended to Euphrates. These were the two northern crowns. 1. David began with the Syrians of Zobah, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3-2Sam.8.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. As he went to settle his border at the river Euphrates (for so far the land conveyed by the divine grant to Abraham and his seed did extend, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">Gen. xv. 18</reference>), the king of Zobah opposed him, being himself possessed of those countries which belonged to Israel; but David routed his forces, and took his chariots and horsemen. The horsemen are here said to be 700, but <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.4">1 Chron. xviii. 4</reference> they are said to be 7000. If they divided their horse by ten in a company, as it is probable they did, the captains and companies were 700, but the horsemen were 7000. David houghed the horses, cut the sinews of their hams, and so lamed them, and made them unserviceable, at least in war, God having forbidden them to <hi type="italic">multiply horses,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.17.16">Deut. xvii. 16</reference>. David reserved only 100 chariots out of 1000 for his own use: for he placed his strength not in chariots nor horses, but in the living God (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Ps. xx. 7</reference>), and wrote it from his own observation that a <hi type="italic">horse is a vain thing for safety,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.33.16-Ps.33.17">Ps. xxxiii. 16, 17</reference>. 2. The Syrians of Damascus coming in to the relief of the king of Zobah fell with him. 22,000 were slain in the field, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.5">v. 5</reference>. So that it was easy for David to make himself master of the country, and garrison it for himself, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.6">v. 6</reference>. The enemies of God's church, that think to secure themselves, will prove, in the end, to ruin themselves, by their confederacies with each other. <hi type="italic">Associate yourselves, and you shall be broken in pieces,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.8.9">Isa. viii. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen6112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6113" type="x-p"/> IV. In all these wars, 1. David was protected: <hi type="italic">The Lord preserved him whithersoever he went.</hi> It seems, he went in person, and, in the cause of God and Israel, jeoparded his own life in the high places of the field; but God covered his head in the day of battle, which he often speaks of, in his psalms, to the glory of God. 2. He was enriched. He took the shields of gold which the servants of Hadadezer had in their custody (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.7">v. 7</reference>) and much brass from several cities of Syria (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.8">v. 8</reference>), which he was entitled to, not only <hi type="italic">jure belli—by the uncontrollable right of the longest sword</hi> ("Get it, and take it"); but by commission from heaven, and the ancient entail of these countries on the seed of Abraham.
entries.46fab2f53f1725dd4114b4c11159e9f23077f8d6: <div eID="gen6113" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Conquers Edom. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1042.)</title> <div sID="gen6114" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had smitten all the host of Hadadezer, <hi type="super">10</hi> Then Toi sent Joram his son unto king David, to salute him, and to bless him, because he had fought against Hadadezer, and smitten him: for Hadadezer had wars with Toi. And <hi type="italic">Joram</hi> brought with him vessels of silver, and vessels of gold, and vessels of brass: <hi type="super">11</hi> Which also king David did dedicate unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , with the silver and gold that he had dedicated of all nations which he subdued; <hi type="super">12</hi> Of Syria, and of Moab, and of the children of Ammon, and of the Philistines, and of Amalek, and of the spoil of Hadadezer, son of Rehob, king of Zobah. <hi type="super">13</hi> And David gat <hi type="italic">him</hi> a name when he returned from smiting of the Syrians in the valley of salt, <hi type="italic">being</hi> eighteen thousand <hi type="italic">men.</hi> <hi type="super">14</hi> And he put garrisons in Edom; throughout all Edom put he garrisons, and all they of Edom became David's servants. And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> preserved David whithersoever he went. <div eID="gen6114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6115" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The court made to David by the king of Hamath, who, it seems was at this time at war with the king of Zobah. He hearing of David's success against his enemy, sent his own son ambassador to him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.9-2Sam.8.10">v. 9, 10</reference>), to congratulate him on his victory, to return him thanks for the favour he had done him in breaking the power of one he was in fear of, and to beg his friendship. Thus he not only secured but strengthened himself. And David lost nothing by taking this little prince under his protection, any more than the old Romans did by the like policy; for the wealth he had from the countries he conquered by way of spoil he had from this by way of present or gratuity: <hi type="italic">Vessels of silver and gold.</hi> Better get by composition than by compulsion. 2. The offering David made to God of the spoils of the nations and all the rich things that were brought him. He dedicated all to the Lord, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.11-2Sam.8.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. This crowned all his victories, and made them far to out-shine Alexander's or Caesar's, that they sought their own glory, but he aimed at the glory of God. All the precious things he was master of were dedicated things, that is, they were designed for the building of the temple; and a good omen it was of kindness to the Gentiles in the fulness of time, and of the making of God's house a house of prayer for all people, that the temple was built of the spoils and presents of Gentile nations, in allusion to which we find <hi type="italic">the kings of the earth</hi> bringing <hi type="italic">their glory and honour into the new Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.21.24">Rev. xxi. 24</reference>. Their gods of gold David burnt (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.21">2 Sam. v. 21</reference>), but their vessels of gold he dedicated. Thus in the conquest of a soul, by the grace of the Son of David, what stands in opposition to God must be destroyed, every lust mortified and crucified, but what may glorify him must be dedicated and the property of it altered. Even the merchandise and the hire must be <hi type="italic">holiness to the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.18">Isa. xxiii. 18</reference>), the gain <hi type="italic">consecrated to the Lord of the whole earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.13">Mic. iv. 13</reference>), and then it is truly our own and that most comfortably. 3. The reputation he got, in a particular manner, by his victory over the Syrians and their allies the Edomites, who acted in conjunction with them, as appears by comparing the title of the 60th Psalm, which was penned on this occasion, with <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.13">v. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">He got himself a name</hi> for all that conduct and courage which are the praise of a great and distinguished general. Something extraordinary, it is likely, there was in that action, which turned very much to his honour, yet he is careful to transfer the honour to God, as appears by the psalm he penned on this occasion, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.12">v. 12</reference>. It is through God that we do valiantly. 4. His success against the Edomites. They all became David's servants, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.14">v. 14</reference>. Now, and not till now, Isaac's blessing was accomplished, by which Jacob was made Esau's Lord (<reference osisRef="Gen.27.37-Gen.27.40">Gen. xxvii. 37-40</reference>) and the Edomites continued long tributary to the kings of Judah, as the Moabites were to the kings of Israel, till, in Joram's time, they revolted (<reference osisRef="2Chr.21.8">2 Chron. xxi. 8</reference>) as Isaac had there foretold that Esau should, in process of time, break the yoke from off his neck. Thus David by his conquests, (1.) Secured peace to his son, that he might have time to build the temple. And, (2.) Procured wealth for his son, that he might have wherewith to build it. God employs his servants variously, some in one employment, others in another, some in the spiritual battles, others in the spiritual buildings; and one prepares work for the other, that God may have the glory of all. All David's victories were typical of the success of the gospel against the kingdom of Satan, in which the Son of David rode forth, conquering and to conquer, and he shall reign till he has brought down all opposing rule, principality, and power: and he has, as David had (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">v. 2</reference>), a line to kill and a line to save; for the same gospel is to some a savour of life unto life, to others a savour of death unto death.
entries.d6e0ec2e38aacbddc1282f856b242a14cea8c660: <div eID="gen6115" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Administration of the Government of Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1042.)</title> <div sID="gen6116" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And David reigned over all Israel; and David executed judgment and justice unto all his people. <hi type="super">16</hi> And Joab the son of Zeruiah <hi type="italic">was</hi> over the host; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud <hi type="italic">was</hi> recorder; <hi type="super">17</hi> And Zadok the son of Ahitub, and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar, <hi type="italic">were</hi> the priests; and Seraiah <hi type="italic">was</hi> the scribe; <hi type="super">18</hi> And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada <hi type="italic">was over</hi> both the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and David's sons were chief rulers. <div eID="gen6116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6117" type="x-p"/> David was not so engaged in his wars abroad as to neglect the administration of the government at home. <div eID="gen6117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6118" type="x-p"/> I. His care extended itself to all the parts of his dominion: <hi type="italic">He reigned over all Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.15">v. 15</reference>); not only he had a right to reign over all the tribes, but he did so; they were all safe under his protection, and shared in the fruits of his good government. <div eID="gen6118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6119" type="x-p"/> II. He did justice with an unbiased unshaken hand: <hi type="italic">He executed judgment unto all his people,</hi> neither did wrong nor denied or delayed right to any. This intimates, 1. His industry and close application to business, his easiness of access and readiness to admit all addresses and appeals made to him. All his people, even the meanest, and those too of the meanest tribes, were welcome to his council-board. 2. His impartiality and the equity of his proceedings, in administering justice. He never perverted justice through favour or affection, nor had respect of persons in judgment. Herein he was a type of Christ, who was faithful and true, and who doth <hi type="italic">in righteousness both judge and make war,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.11">Rev. xix. 11</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Ps.72.1-Ps.72.2">Ps. lxxii. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen6119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6120" type="x-p"/> III. He kept good order and good officers in his court. David being the first king that had an established government (for Saul's reign was short and unsettled) he had the modelling of the administration. In Saul's time we read of no other great officer than Abner, that was captain of the host. But David appointed more officers: Joab that was general of the forces in the field, and Banaiah that was over the Cherethites and Pelethites, who were either the city train-bands (<hi type="italic">archers and slingers,</hi> so the Chaldee), or rather the life-guards, or standing force, that attended the king's person, the pretorian band, the militia. They were ready to do service at home, to assist in the administering of justice, and to preserve the public peace. We find them employed in proclaiming Solomon, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.38">1 Kings i. 38</reference>. 2. Two ecclesiastical officers: <hi type="italic">Zadok and Ahimelech were priests,</hi> that is, they were most employed in the priests' work under Abiathar, the high priest. 3. Two civil officers: one that was recorder, or remembrancer, to put the king in mind of business in its season (he was prime minister of state, yet not entrusted with the custody of the king's conscience, as they say of our lord chancellor, but only of the king's memory; let the king be put in mind of business and he would do it himself); another that was scribe, or secretary of state, that drew up public orders and despatches, and recorded judgments given. 4. David's sons, as they grew up to be fit for business, were made chief rulers; they had places of honour and trust assigned them, in the household, or in the camp, or in the courts of justice, according as their genius led them. They were chief about the king (so it is explained, <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.17">1 Chron. xviii. 17</reference>), employed near him, that they might be under his eye. Our Lord Jesus has appointed officers in his kingdom, for his honour and the good of the community; when he ascended on high <hi type="italic">he gave these gifts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.8-Eph.4.11">Eph. iv. 8-11</reference>), <hi type="italic">to every man his work,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.13.34">Mark xiii. 34</reference>. David made his sons chief rulers; but all believers, Christ's spiritual seed, are better preferred, for they are <hi type="italic">made to our God kings and priests,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.6">Rev. i. 6</reference>.  <chapter eID="2Sam.8"/> <div eID="gen6120" type="x-p"/>

entries.d47be956e7fb0f6559c366c2ee15d91e5621b787: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2890"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 8</title> <div sID="gen3980" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.1">2Sa 8:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.2">2</reference>. David Subdues the Philistines, and Makes the Moabites Tributary.<div eID="gen3980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3981" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2890"/><hi type="bold">1. David took Metheg-ammah out of the hand of the Philistines--</hi>that is, Gath and her suburban towns (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.1">1Ch 18:1</reference>). That town had been "a bridle" by which the Philistines kept the people of Judah in check. David used it now as a barrier to repress that restless enemy. <div eID="gen3981" type="x-p"/>
entries.67087e30abbca99e5f51d4b6132a694b6e676fd4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2891"/><div sID="gen3982" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2891"/><hi type="bold">2. he smote Moab, and measured them with a line--</hi>This refers to a well-known practice of Eastern kings, to command their prisoners of war, particularly those who, notorious for the atrocity of their crimes or distinguished by the indomitable spirit of their resistance, had greatly incensed the victors, to lie down on the ground. Then a certain portion of them, which was determined by lot, but most commonly by a measuring-line, were put to death. Our version makes him put two-thirds to death, and spare one-third. The Septuagint and Vulgate make one-half. This war usage was not, perhaps, usually practised by the people of God; but Jewish writers assert that the cause of this particular severity against this people was their having massacred David's parents and family, whom he had, during his exile, committed to the king of Moab.<div eID="gen3982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3983" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3-2Sam.8.14">2Sa 8:3-14</reference>. He Smites Hadadezer and the Syrians. <div eID="gen3983" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a20c6626a066c71eaa3a2e4eb1b15bb0c51a50b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2892"/><div sID="gen3984" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2892"/><hi type="bold">3. Zobah--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.3">1Ch 18:3</reference>). This kingdom was bounded on the east by the Euphrates, and it extended westward from that river, perhaps as far north as Aleppo. It was long the chief among the petty kingdoms of Syria, and its king bore the hereditary title of "Hadadezer" or "Hadarezer" ("Hadad," that is, "helped").<div eID="gen3984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3985" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as he went to recover his border at the river Euphrates--</hi>in accordance with the promises God made to Israel that He would give them all the country as far as the Euphrates (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">Ge 15:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.24.17">Nu 24:17</reference>). In the first campaign David signally defeated Hadadezer. Besides a great number of foot prisoners, he took from him an immense amount of booty in chariots and horses. Reserving only a small number of the latter, he hamstrung the rest. The horses were thus mutilated because they were forbidden to the Hebrews, both in war and agriculture. So it was of no use to keep them. Besides, their neighbors placed much dependence on cavalry, but having, for want of a native breed, to procure them by purchase, the greatest damage that could be done to such enemies was to render their horses unserviceable in war. (See also <reference osisRef="Gen.46.6">Ge 46:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.11.6">Jos 11:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.9">9</reference>). A king of Damascene-Syria came to Hadadezer's succor; but David routed those auxiliary forces also, took possession of their country, put garrisons into their fortified towns, and made them tributary. <div eID="gen3985" type="x-p"/>
entries.e236b7a6ab6dc950aecb1114105c8c7caf62dd38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2893"/><div sID="gen3986" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2893"/><hi type="bold">9. Toi king of Hamath--</hi>Coele-Syria; northwards, it extended to the city Hamath on the Orontes, which was the capital of the country. The Syrian prince, being delivered from the dread of a dangerous neighbor, sent his son with valuable presents to David to congratulate him on his victories, and solicit his alliance and protection. <div eID="gen3986" type="x-p"/>
entries.c76e694dc0b207b1246831811f89115a1dd4a42d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2894"/><div sID="gen3987" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2894"/><hi type="bold">10. Joram--</hi>or Hadoram (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.10">1Ch 18:10</reference>). <div eID="gen3987" type="x-p"/>
entries.f0dffcd3893968e0d8f819aa68377cf3a932db61: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2895"/><div sID="gen3988" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2895"/><hi type="bold">11. Which also king David did dedicate unto the Lord--</hi>Eastern princes have always been accustomed to hoard up vast quantities of gold. This is the first instance of a practice uniformly followed by David of reserving, after defraying expenses and bestowing suitable rewards upon his soldiers, the remainder of the spoil taken in war, to accumulate for the grand project of his life--the erection of a national temple at Jerusalem. <div eID="gen3988" type="x-p"/>
entries.aceb50dfab10a43fcf40e5c1fc6892287b22e7b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2896"/><div sID="gen3989" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2896"/><hi type="bold">13. David gat him a name when he returned from smiting of the Syrians--</hi>Instead of Syrians, the Septuagint version reads "Edomites," which is the true reading, as is evident from <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.14">2Sa 8:14</reference>. This conquest, made by the army of David, was due to the skilful generalship and gallantry of Abishai and Joab. (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.12">1Ch 18:12</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.60.1">Psa 60:1</reference>, title.) The valley was the ravine of salt (the Ghor), adjoining the Salt Mountain, at the southwestern extremity of the Dead Sea, separating the ancient territories of Judah and Edom [Robinson].<div eID="gen3989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3990" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.15-2Sam.8.18">2Sa 8:15-18</reference>. His Reign. <div eID="gen3990" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf7540ca68d34b1ac6101730d6e51f60b901f514: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2897"/><div sID="gen3991" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2897"/><hi type="bold">15. David executed judgment and justice unto all his people--</hi>Though involved in foreign wars, he maintained an excellent system of government at home, the most eminent men of the age composing his cabinet of ministers. <div eID="gen3991" type="x-p"/>
entries.45adbd48c3d3ecc8a6c3a4aacaa61aad7a13caae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2898"/><div sID="gen3992" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2898"/><hi type="bold">16. Joab ... was over the host--</hi>by virtue of a special promise (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.8">2Sa 5:8</reference>).<div eID="gen3992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3993" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">recorder--</hi>historiographer or daily annalist, an office of great trust and importance in Eastern countries. <div eID="gen3993" type="x-p"/>
entries.241144cf316e6b73e02b25fe33432f75068e737b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2899"/><div sID="gen3994" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2899"/><hi type="bold">17. Zadok ... and Ahimelech ... were the priests--</hi>On the massacre of the priests at Nob, [1Sa 22:19], Saul conferred the priesthood on Zadok, of the family of Eleazar (<reference osisRef="1Chr.6.50">1Ch 6:50</reference>), while David acknowledged Ahimelech, of Ithamar's family, who fled to him. The two high priests exercised their office under the respective princes to whom they were attached. But, on David's obtaining the kingdom over all Israel, they both retained their dignity; Ahimelech officiating at Jerusalem, and Zadok at Gibeon (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.39">1Ch 16:39</reference>). <div eID="gen3994" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ad01621c11ce36c5ac116856646cb18d2a86639: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2900"/><div sID="gen3995" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2900"/><hi type="bold">18. Cherethites--</hi>that is, Philistines (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.5">Zep 2:5</reference>).<div eID="gen3995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3996" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Pelethites--</hi>from Pelet (<reference osisRef="1Chr.12.3">1Ch 12:3</reference>). They were the valiant men who, having accompanied David during his exile among the Philistines, were made his bodyguard. <chapter eID="2Sam.8"/>

entries.0869a7dd0d08bf8708aee39f9e9f055403cf86ae: <div eID="gen10875" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10876" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10877" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10877" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10876" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10878" type="x-p"/> David subdues the Philistines, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.1">2Sam 8:1</reference>; and the Moabites, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">2Sam 8:2</reference>; and the king of Zobah, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3">2Sam 8:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.4">2Sam 8:4</reference>; and the Syrians in general, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.5-2Sam.8.8">2Sam 8:5-8</reference>. Toi, king of Hamath, sends to congratulate him on his victories over the king of Zobah, and sends him rich presents, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.9-2Sam.8.10">2Sam 8:9-10</reference>. David dedicates all the spoils to God, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.11-2Sam.8.13">2Sam 8:11-13</reference>. He garrisons Edom, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.14">2Sam 8:14</reference>; and reigns over all Israel, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.15">2Sam 8:15</reference>. An account of his chief officers, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.16-2Sam.8.18">2Sam 8:16-18</reference>. <div eID="gen10878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10879" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10880" type="x-p"/> David took Metheg-ammah - This is variously translated. The Vulgate has, Tulit David fraenum tributi, David removed the bondage of the tribute, which the Israelites paid to the Philistines. Some think it means a fortress, city, or strong town; but no such place as Metheg-ammah is known. Probably the Vulgate is nearest the truth. The versions are all different. See the following comparison of the principal passages here collated with the parallel place in 1 Chr: - 2 Samuel 1 Chronicles <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.1">2Sam 8:1</reference>. - David took Metheg-ammah <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3">2Sam 8:3</reference>.
