entries.c1e712c3204e100c323d53e5c6a5141f28dbecc5: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10881" type="x-p"/> And measured them with a line - even with two lines - It has been generally conjectured that David, after he had conquered Moab, consigned two-thirds of the inhabitants to the sword; but I think the text will bear a meaning much more reputable to that king. The first clause of the verse seems to determine the sense; he measured them with a line, casting them down to the ground - to put to death, and with one line to keep alive. Death seems here to be referred to the cities by way of metaphor; and, from this view of the subject we may conclude that two-thirds of the cities, that is, the strong places of Moab, were erased; and not having strong places to trust to, the text adds, So the Moabites became David's servants, and brought gifts, i.e., were obliged to pay tribute. The word line may mean the same here as our rod, i.e., the instrument by which land is measured. There are various opinions on this verse, with which I shall not trouble the reader. Much may be seen in Calmet and Dodd.
entries.f709eaf01b4a00cf1a445dfef928473483aeb8d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen10881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10882" type="x-p"/> David smote - Hadadezer - He is supposed to have been king of all Syria, except Phoenicia; and, wishing to extend his dominions to the Euphrates, invaded a part of David's dominions which lay contiguous to it; but being attacked by David, he was totally routed.
entries.5d8ce411716a8de91d1ed67937825d1b8e41ef37: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen10882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10883" type="x-p"/> A thousand chariots - It is strange that there were a thousand chariots, and only seven hundred horsemen taken, and twenty thousand foot. But as the discomfiture appears complete, we may suppose that the chariots, being less manageable, might be more easily taken, while the horsemen might, in general, make their escape. The infantry also seem to have been surrounded, when twenty thousand of them were taken prisoners. <div eID="gen10883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10884" type="x-p"/> David houghed all the chariot horses - If he did so, it was both unreasonable and inhuman; for, as he had so complete a victory, there was no danger of these horses falling into the enemy's hands; and if he did not choose to keep them, which indeed the law would not permit, he should have killed them outright; and then the poor innocent creatures would have been put out of pain. But does the text speak of houghing horses at all? It does not. Let us hear; ויעקר דוד את כל הרכב vayeakker David eth col harecheb, And David disjointed all the chariots, except a hundred chariots which he reserved for himself. Now, this destruction of the chariots, was a matter of sound policy, and strict piety. God had censured those who trusted in chariots; piety therefore forbade David the use of them: and lest they should fall into the enemy's hands, and be again used against him, policy induced him to destroy them. The Septuagint render the words nearly as I have done, και παρελυσε Δαυιδ παντα τα ἁρματα. <div eID="gen10884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10885" type="x-p"/> He kept however one hundred; probably as a sort of baggage or forage wagons.
entries.b50c74a423db20554453a1a9df663b58327410d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10886" type="x-p"/> Brought gifts - Paid tribute.
entries.97af124100d9e25e57a8d43fe396befca44df188: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen10886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10887" type="x-p"/> David took the shields of gold - We know not what these were. Some translate arms, others quivers, others bracelets, others collars, and others shields. They were probably costly ornaments by which the Syrian soldiers were decked and distinguished. And those who are called servants here, were probably the choice troops or body-guard of Hadadezer, as the argyraspides were of Alexander the Great. See Quintus Curtius.
entries.c540f726f1b08ac44b9632aadd1dd4e7f0199396: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen10887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10888" type="x-p"/> Toi king of Hamath - Hamath is supposed to be the famous city of Emesa, situated on the Orontes, in Syria. This was contiguous to <div eID="gen10888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10889" type="x-p"/> Hadadezer; and led him to wage war with Toi, that he might get possession of his territories. For a comparison of the 10th verse, see <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.9">1Chr 18:9</reference>.
entries.103e006d26604e99394cd68328e79ebe1677e894: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen10889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10890" type="x-p"/> David gat him a name - Became a very celebrated and eminent man. The Targum has it, David collected troops; namely, to recruit his army when he returned from smiting the Syrians. His many battles had no doubt greatly thinned his army. <div eID="gen10890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10891" type="x-p"/> The valley of salt - Supposed to be a large plain abounding in this mineral, about a league from the city of Palmyra or Tadmor in the wilderness.
entries.e79d6334ace490d45536c81070b3b523b1c09774: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen10891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10892" type="x-p"/> He put garrisons in Edom - He repaired the strong cities which he had taken, and put garrisons in them to keep the country in awe.
entries.9ef0654e1fa8317808bba1b74154baf99ac92e8d: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen10892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10893" type="x-p"/> Joab - was over the host - General and commander-in-chief over all the army. <div eID="gen10893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10894" type="x-p"/> Ahilud - recorder - מזכיר mazkir, remembrancer; one who kept a strict journal of all the proceedings of the king and operations of his army; a chronicler. Or, remembrancer, or, writer of chronicles.
entries.e6f7a59bb75a41787da5026b07d1cc73cbca54be: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen10894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10895" type="x-p"/> Seraiah - the scribe - Most likely the king's private secretary. See <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.3">1Chr 24:3</reference> (note).
entries.a07e2f9150149319233575ba68bbb3ffb8f95ba4: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen10895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10896" type="x-p"/> Benaiah - The chief of the second class of David's worthies. We shall meet with him again. <div eID="gen10896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10897" type="x-p"/> The Cherethites and the Pelethites - The former supposed to be those who accompanied David when he fled from Saul; the latter, those who came to him at Ziklag. But the Targum translates these two names thus, the archers and the slingers; and this is by far the most likely. It is not at all probable that David was without a company both of archers and slingers. The bow is celebrated in the funeral lamentation over Saul and Jonathan; and the sling was renowned as the weapon of the Israelites, and how expert David was in the use of it we learn from the death of Goliath. I take for granted that the Chaldee paraphrast is correct. No weapons then known were equally powerful with these; the spears, swords, and javelins, of other nations, were as stubble before them. The bow was the grand weapon of our English ancestors; and even after the invention of firearms, they were with difficulty persuaded to prefer them and leave their archery.  <chapter eID="2Sam.8"/> <div eID="gen10897" type="x-p"/>

entries.b0e799d793dbc73b808ecd9ce999abbc3f7aedaf: <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.1">2Sa 8:1</reference> <div eID="gen4334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4335" type="x-p"/> Subjugation of the Philistines. - In the introductory formula, <hi type="italic">“And it came to pass afterwards,”</hi> the expression <hi type="italic">“afterwards”</hi> cannot refer specially to the contents of 2 Samuel 7, for reasons also given, but simply serves as a general formula of transition to attach what follows to the account just completed, as a thing that happened afterwards. This is incontestably evident from a comparison of <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.1">2Sa 10:1</reference>, where the war with the Ammonites and Syrians, the termination and result of which are given in the present chapter, is attached to what precedes by the same formula, <hi type="italic">“It came to pass afterwards”</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.13.1">2Sa 13:1</reference>). <hi type="italic">“David smote the Philistines and subdued them, and took the bridle of the mother out of the hand of the Philistines,”</hi> i.e., wrested the government from them and made them tributary. The figurative expression <hi type="italic">Metheg-ammah</hi>, “bridle of the mother,” i.e., the capital, has been explained by Alb. Schultens (on <reference osisRef="Job.30.11">Job 30:11</reference>) from an Arabic idiom, in which giving up one’s bridle to another is equivalent to submitting to him. Gesenius also gives several proofs of this (<hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 113). Others, for example Ewald, render it arm-bridle; but there is not a single passage to support the rendering “arm” for <hi type="italic">ammah</hi>. The word is a feminine form of אם, mother, and only used in a tropical sense. <hi type="italic">“Mother”</hi> is a term applied to the chief city or capital, both in Arabic and Phoenician (vid., Ges<hi type="italic">.</hi> <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 112). The same figure is also adopted in Hebrew, where the towns dependent upon the capital are called its daughters (vid., <reference osisRef="Josh.15.45">Jos 15:45</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.47">Jos 15:47</reference>). In <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.1">1Ch 18:1</reference> the figurative expression is dropped for the more literal one: “David took Gath and its daughters out of the hand of the Philistines,” i.e., he wrested Gath and the other towns from the Philistines. The Philistines had really five cities, every one with a prince of its own (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.3">Jos 13:3</reference>). This was the case even in the time of Samuel (<reference osisRef="1Sam.6.16-1Sam.6.17">1Sa 6:16-17</reference>). But in the closing years of Samuel, Gath had a <hi type="italic">king</hi> who stood at the head of all the princes of the Philistines (1Sa 29:2., cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.2">1Sa 27:2</reference>). Thus Gath became the capital of the land of the Philistines, which held the bridle (or reins) of Philistia in its own hand. The author of the Chronicles has therefore given the correct explanation of the figure. The one suggested by <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, Bertheau, and others, cannot be correct, - namely, that David wrested from the Philistines the power which they had hitherto exercised over the Israelites. The simple meaning of the passage is, that David wrested from the Philistines the power which the capital had possessed over the towns dependent upon it, i.e., over the whole of the land of Philistia; in other words, he brought the capital (Gath) and the other towns of Philistia into his own power. The reference afterwards made to a king of Gath in the time of Solomon in 1Ki 2:39 is by no means at variance with this; for the king alluded to was one of the tributary sovereigns, as we may infer from the fact that Solomon ruled over all the kings on this side of the Euphrates as far as to Gaza (1Ki 5:1, 1Ki 5:4).
entries.419b3b676794330384ed8f9c4bad99b0b583f192: <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">2Sa 8:2</reference> <div eID="gen4335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4336" type="x-p"/> Subjugation of Moab. - <hi type="italic">“He smote Moab </hi>(i.e., the Moabites),<hi type="italic">and measured them with the line, making them lie down upon the ground, and measured two lines </hi>(i.e., two parts)<hi type="italic">to put to death, and one line full to keep alive.”</hi> Nothing further is known about either the occasion or the history of this war, with the exception of the cursory notice in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.22">1Ch 11:22</reference>, that Benaiah, one of David’s heroes, smote two sons of the king of Moab, which no doubt took place in the same war. In the earliest period of his flight from Saul, David had met with a hospitable reception from the king of Moab, and had even taken his parents to him for safety (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.3-1Sam.22.4">1Sa 22:3-4</reference>). But the Moabites must have very grievously oppressed the Israelites afterwards, that David should have inflicted a severer punishment upon them after their defeat, than upon any other of the nations that he conquered, with the exception of the Ammonites (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.31">2Sa 12:31</reference>), upon whom he took vengeance for having most shamefully insulted his ambassadors (2Sa 10:2.). The punishment inflicted, however, was of course restricted to the fighting men who had been taken prisoners by the Israelites. They were ordered to lie down in a row upon the earth; and then the row was measured for the purpose of putting two-thirds to death, and leaving one-third alive. The Moabites were then made <hi type="italic">“servants”</hi> to David (i.e., they became his subjects), <hi type="italic">“bringing gifts”</hi> (i.e., paying tribute).
entries.eb25e1a35ba84f103cb2903cc26e79e228a6edef: <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3-2Sam.8.4">2Sa 8:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen4336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4337" type="x-p"/> Conquest and Subjugation of the King of Zobah, and of the Damascene Syrians. - 2Sa 8:3. The situation of <hi type="italic">Zobah</hi> cannot be determined. The view held by the Syrian church historians, and defended by Michaelis, viz., that <hi type="italic">Zobah</hi> was the ancient <hi type="italic">Nisibis</hi> in northern Mesopotamia, has no more foundation to rest upon than that of certain Jewish writers who suppose it to have been <hi type="italic">Aleppo</hi>, the present <hi type="italic">Haleb</hi>. <hi type="italic">Aleppo</hi> is too far north for <hi type="italic">Zobah</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Nisibis</hi> is quite out of the range of the towns and tribes in connection with which the name of Zobah occurs. In <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.47">1Sa 14:47</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.12">2Sa 8:12</reference> of this chapter, Zobah, or <hi type="italic">Aram Zobah</hi> as it is called in <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.6">2Sa 10:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.60.2">Psa 60:2</reference>, is mentioned along with Ammon, Moab, and Edom, as a neighbouring tribe and kingdom to the Israelites; and, according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3">2Sa 8:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.5">2Sa 8:5</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.9">2Sa 8:9</reference> of the present chapter, it is to be sought for in the vicinity of Damascus and Hamath towards the Euphrates. These data point to a situation to the north-east of Damascus and south of Hamath, between the Orontes and Euphrates, and in fact extending as far as the latter according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3">2Sa 8:3</reference>, whilst, according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.16">2Sa 10:16</reference>, it even reached beyond it with its vassal-chiefs into Mesopotamia itself. Ewald (<hi type="italic">Gesch</hi>. iii. p. 195) has therefore combined <hi type="italic">Zobah</hi>, which was no doubt the capital, and gave its name to the kingdom, with the <hi type="italic">Sabe</hi> mentioned in Ptol. v. 19, - a town in the same latitude as Damascus, and farther east towards the Euphrates. The king of Zobah at the time referred to is called <hi type="italic">Hadadezer</hi> in the text (i.e., whose help is <hi type="italic">Hadad</hi>); but in <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.16-2Sam.10.19">2Sa 10:16-19</reference> and throughout the Chronicles he is called <hi type="italic">Hadarezer</hi>. The first is the original form; for <hi type="italic">Hadad</hi>, the name of the sun-god of the Syrians, is met with in several other instances in Syrian names (vid., Movers, <hi type="italic">Phönizier</hi>). David smote this king “<hi type="italic">as he was going to restore his strength at the river</hi> (Euphrates).” ידו השׁיב does not mean to turn his hand, but signifies to return his hand, to stretch it out again over or against any one, in all the passage in which the expression occurs. It is therefore to be taken in a derivative sense in the passage before us, and signifying to restore or re-establish his sway. The expression used in the Chronicles (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.3">2Sa 8:3</reference>), ידו הצּיב, has just the same meaning, since establishing or making fast presupposes a previous weakening or dissolution. Hence the subject of the sentence “as he went,” etc., must be Hadadezer and not David; for David could not have extended his power to the Euphrates before the defeat of Hadadezer. The Masoretes have interpolated <hi type="italic">P'rath</hi> (Euphrates) after <hi type="italic">“the river,”</hi> as in the text of the Chronicles. This is correct enough so far as the sense is concerned, but it is by no means necessary, as the <hi type="italic">nahar</hi> (the river κ. ἐξ.) is quite sufficient of itself to indicate the Euphrates. <div eID="gen4337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4338" type="x-p"/> There is also a war between David and Hadadezer and other kings of Syria mentioned in 2 Samuel 10; and the commentators all admit that that war, in which David defeated these kings when they came to the help of the Ammonites, is connected with the war mentioned in the present chapter. But the connection is generally supposed to be this, that the first of David’s Aramaean wars is given in 2 Samuel 8, the second in 2 Samuel 10; for no other reason, however, than because 2 Samuel 10 stands after 2 Samuel 8. This view is decidedly an erroneous one. According to the chapter before us, the war mentioned there terminated in the complete subjugation of the Aramaean kings and kingdoms. Aram became subject to David, paying tribute (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.6">2Sa 8:6</reference>). Now, though the revolt of subjugated nations from their conquerors is by no means a rare thing in history, and therefore it is perfectly conceivable in itself that the Aramaeans should have fallen away from David when he was involved in the war with the Ammonites, and should have gone to the help of the Ammonites, such an assumption is precluded by the fact that there is nothing in 2 Samuel 10 about any falling away or revolt of the Aramaeans from David; but, on the contrary, these tribes appear to be still entirely independent of David, and to be hired by the Ammonites to fight against him. But what is absolutely decisive against this assumption, is the fact that the number of Aramaeans killed in the two wars is precisely the same (compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.4">2Sa 8:4</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.18">2Sa 10:18</reference>): so that it may safely be inferred, not only that the war mentioned in 2 Samuel 10, in which the Aramaeans who had come to the help of the Ammonites were smitten by David, was the very same as the Aramaean war mentioned in 2 Samuel 8, but of which the result only is given; but also that all the wars which David waged with the Aramaeans, like his war with Edom (2Sa 8:13.), arose out of the Ammonitish war (2 Samuel 10), and the fact that the Ammonites enlisted the help of the kings of Aram against David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.6">2Sa 10:6</reference>). We also obtain from 2 Samuel 10 an explanation of the expression “as he went to restore his power (Eng. Ver. 'recover his border') at the river,” since it is stated there that Hadadezer was defeated by Joab the first time, and that, after sustaining this defeat, he called the Aramaeans on the other side of the Euphrates to his assistance, that he might continue the war against Israel with renewed vigour (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.13">2Sa 10:13</reference>, 2Sa 10:15.). The power of Hadadezer had no doubt been crippled by his first defeat; and in order to restore it, he procured auxiliary troops from Mesopotamia with which to attack David, but he was defeated a second time, and obliged to submit to him (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.17-2Sam.10.18">2Sa 10:17-18</reference>). In this second engagement <hi type="italic">“David took from him </hi>(i.e., captured)<hi type="italic">seventeen hundred horse-soldiers and twenty thousand foot”</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.4">2Sa 8:4</reference>, compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.18">2Sa 10:18</reference>). This decisive battle took place, according to <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.3">1Ch 18:3</reference>, in the neighbourhood of <hi type="italic">Hamath</hi>, i.e., Epiphania on the Orontes (see at Num 13:21, and <reference osisRef="Gen.10.18">Gen 10:18</reference>), or, according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.18">2Sa 10:18</reference> of this book, at <hi type="italic">Helam</hi>, - a difference which may easily be reconciled by the simple assumption that the unknown Helam was somewhere near to Hamath. Instead of 1700 horse-soldiers, we find in the Chronicles (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.4">1Ch 18:4</reference>) 1000 chariots and 7000 horsemen. Consequently the word receb has no doubt dropped out after אלף in the text before us, and the numeral denoting a thousand has been confounded with the one used to denote a hundred; for in the plains of Syria seven thousand horsemen would be a much juster proportion to twenty thousand foot than seventeen hundred. (For further remarks, see at 2Sa 10:18.) <hi type="italic">“And David lamed all the cavalry,”</hi> i.e., he made the war-chariots and cavalry perfectly useless by laming the horses (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.11.6">Jos 11:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.9">Jos 11:9</reference>), - <hi type="italic">“and only left a hundred horses.”</hi> The word <hi type="italic">receb</hi> in these clauses signifies the war-horses generally, - not merely the carriage-horses, but the riding-horses as well, - as the meaning cavalry is placed beyond all doubt by <reference osisRef="Isa.21.7">Isa 21:7</reference>, and it can hardly be imagined that David would have spared the riding-horses.
entries.b6c7ed909c82331af0e616e9fdf113bdc971873d: <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.5-2Sam.8.6">2Sa 8:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen4338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4339" type="x-p"/> After destroying the main force of Hadadezer, David turned against his ally, against <hi type="italic">Aram-Damascus</hi>, i.e., the Aramaeans, whose capital was Damascus. <hi type="italic">Dammesek</hi> (for which we have <hi type="italic">Darmesek</hi> in the Chronicles according to its Aramaean form), <hi type="italic">Damascus</hi>, a very ancient and still a very important city of Syria, standing upon the <hi type="italic">Chrysorrhoas</hi> (<hi type="italic">Pharpar</hi>), which flows through the centre of it. It is situated in the midst of paradisaical scenery, on the eastern side of the Antilibanus, on the road which unites Western Asia with the interior. David smote 22,000 Syrians of Damascus, placed garrisons in the kingdom, and made it subject and tributary. נציבים are not governors of officers, but military posts, garrisons, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.5">1Sa 10:5</reference>; 1Sa 13:3.
entries.870ead2274efcc1029437e33d0df95a23a35461b: <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.7">2Sa 8:7</reference> <div eID="gen4339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4340" type="x-p"/> Of the booty taken in these wars, David carried the golden shields which he took from the servants, i.e., the governors and vassal princes, of Hadadezer, to Jerusalem.<note placement="foot">The lxx has this additional clause: “And Shishak the king of Egypt took them away, when he went up against Jerusalem in the days of Rehoboam the son of Solomon,” which is neither to be found in the Chronicles nor in any other ancient version, and is merely an inference drawn by the Greek translator, or by some copyists of the lxx, from 1Ki 14:25-28, taken in connection with the fact that the application of the brass is given in 1Ch 18:8. But, in the first place, the author of this gloss has overlooked the fact that the golden shields of Rehoboam which Shishak carried away, were not those captured by David, but those which Solomon had had made, according to 1Ki 10:16, for the retainers of his palace; and in the second place, he has not observed that, according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.11">2Sa 8:11</reference> of this chapter, and also of the Chronicles, David dedicated to the Lord all the gold and silver that he had taken, i.e., put it in the treasury of the sanctuary to be reserved for the future temple, and that at the end of his reign he handed over to his son and successor Solomon all the gold, silver, iron, and brass that he had collected for the purpose, to be applied to the building of the temple (1Ch 22:14., 1Ch 29:2.). Consequently the clause in question, which Thenius would adopt from the lxx into our own text, is nothing more than the production of a presumptuous Alexandrian, whose error lies upon the very surface, so that the question of its genuineness cannot for a moment be entertained.</note><hi type="italic">Shelet</hi> signifies “a shield,” according to the Targums and Rabbins, and this meaning is applicable to all the passages in which the word occurs; whilst the meaning “equivalent” cannot be sustained either by the rendering πανοπλία adopted by Aquila and Symmachus in 2Ki 11:10, or by the renderings of the Vulgate, viz., <hi type="italic">arma</hi> in loc. and <hi type="italic">armatura</hi> in Sol 4:4, or by an appeal to the etymology (vid., Gesenius’ Thes. and Dietrich’s <hi type="italic">Lexicon</hi>).
entries.7e70098b7733000bc39b8e1dde7fac29b5d1417a: <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.8">2Sa 8:8</reference> <div eID="gen4340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4341" type="x-p"/> And from the cities of <hi type="italic">Betach</hi> and <hi type="italic">Berothai</hi> David took very much brass, with which, according to <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.8">1Ch 18:8</reference>, Solomon made the brazen sea, and the brazen columns and vessels of the temple. The lxx have also interpolated this notice into the text. The name <hi type="italic">Betach</hi> is given as <hi type="italic">Tibhath</hi> in the Chronicles; and for <hi type="italic">Berothai</hi> we have <hi type="italic">Chun</hi>. As the towns themselves are unknown, it cannot be decided with certainty which of the forms and names are the correct and original ones. מבּטח appears to have been written by mistake for מטּבח. This supposition is favoured by the rendering of the lxx, ἐκ τῆς Μετεβάκ; and by that of the Syriac also (viz., <hi type="italic">Tebach</hi>). On the other hand, the occurrence of the name <hi type="italic">Tebah</hi> among the sons of <hi type="italic">Nahor the Aramaean</hi> in <reference osisRef="Gen.22.24">Gen 22:24</reference> proves little or nothing, as it is not known that he founded a family which perpetuated his name; nor can anything be inferred from the fact that, according to the more modern maps, there is a town of <hi type="italic">Tayibeh</hi> to the north of Damascus in 35 north lat., as there is very little in common between the names <hi type="italic">Tayibeh</hi> and <hi type="italic">Tebah</hi>. Ewald connects <hi type="italic">Berothai</hi> with the <hi type="italic">Barathena</hi> of Ptol. v. 19 in the neighbourhood of Saba. The connection is a possible one, but it is not sufficiently certain to warrant us in founding any conclusions upon it with regard to the name <hi type="italic">Chun</hi> which occurs in the Chronicles; so that there is no ground whatever for the opinion that it is a corruption of <hi type="italic">Berothai</hi>.
entries.587f9796fd1ed35f42a8de392332b62a06ac98b0: <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.9-2Sam.8.10">2Sa 8:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen4341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4342" type="x-p"/> After the defeat of the king of Zobah and his allies, Toi king of Hamath sought for David’s friendship, sending his son to salute him, and conveying to him at the same time a considerable present of vessels of silver, gold, and brass. The name <hi type="italic">Toi</hi> is written <hi type="italic">Tou</hi> in the Chronicles, according to a different mode of interpretation; and the name of the son is given as <hi type="italic">Hadoram</hi> in the Chronicles, instead of <hi type="italic">Joram</hi> as in the text before us. The former is evidently the true reading, and <hi type="italic">Joram</hi> an error of the pen, as the Israelitish name <hi type="italic">Joram</hi> is not one that we should expect to find among Aramaeans; whilst <hi type="italic">Hadoram</hi> occurs in <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.21">1Ch 1:21</reference> in the midst of Arabic names, and it cannot be shown that the <hi type="italic">Hadoram</hi> or <hi type="italic">Adoram</hi> mentioned in <reference osisRef="2Chr.10.18">2Ch 10:18</reference> and 1Ki 12:18 was a man of Israelitish descent. The primary object of the mission was to salute David (“to ask him of peace;” cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.43.27">Gen 43:27</reference>, etc.), and to congratulate him upon his victory (“to bless him because he had fought,” etc.); for Toi had had wars with Hadadezer. <hi type="italic">“A man of wars”</hi> signifies a man who wages wars (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.3">1Ch 28:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.42.13">Isa 42:13</reference>). According to <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.3">1Ch 18:3</reference>, the territory of the king of Hamath bordered upon that of Hadadezer, and the latter had probably tried to make king Toi submit to him. The secret object of the salutation, however, was no doubt to secure the friendship of this new and powerful neighbour.
entries.72e72501c91acd29062daf3e4a3f1f34f6541106: <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.11-2Sam.8.12">2Sa 8:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen4342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4343" type="x-p"/> David also sanctified Toi’s presents to the Lord (handed them over to the treasury of the sanctuary), together with the silver and gold which he had sanctified from all the conquered nations, from Aram, Moab, etc. Instead of הקדּישׁ אשׁר the text of the Chronicles has נשׂא אשׁר, which he took, i.e., took as booty. Both are equally correct; there is simply a somewhat different turn given to the thought.<note placement="foot">Bertheau erroneously maintains that נשׂא אשׁר, which he took, is at variance with <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.7">2Sa 8:7</reference>, as, according to this passage, the golden shields of Hadadezer did not become the property of the Lord. But there is not a word to that effect in 2Sa 8:7. On the contrary, his taking the shields to Jerusalem implies, rather than precludes, the intention to devote them to the purposes of the sanctuary.</note> <div eID="gen4343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4344" type="x-p"/> In the enumeration of the conquered nations in <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.12">2Sa 8:12</reference>, the text of the Chronicles differs from that of the book before us. In the first place, we find “from Edom” instead of “from Aram;” and secondly, the clause “and of the spoil of Hadadezer, son of Rehob king of Zobah,” is altogether wanting there. The text of the Chronicles is certainly faulty here, as the name of Aram (Syria) could not possibly be omitted. Edom could much better be left out, not “because the conquest of Edom belonged to a later period,” as <hi type="italic">Movers</hi> maintains, but because the conquest of Edom is mentioned for the first time in the subsequent verses. But if we bear in mind that in <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.12">2Sa 8:12</reference> of both texts not only are those tribes enumerated the conquest of which had been already noticed, but all the tribes that David ever defeated and subjugated, even the Ammonites and Amalekites, to the war with whom no allusion whatever is made in the present chapter, we shall see that Edom could not be omitted. Consequently “from Syria” must have dropped out of the text of the Chronicles, and “from Edom” out of the one before us; so that the text in both instances ran originally thus, “from Syria, and from Edom, and from Moab.” For even in the text before us, “from Aram” (Syria) could not well be omitted, notwithstanding the fact that the booty of Hadadezer is specially mentioned at the close of the verse, for the simple reason that David not only made war upon Syria-Zobah (the kingdom of Hadadezer) and subdued it, but also upon Syria-Damascus, which was quite independent of Zobah.
entries.84bc1887059baacc218406214cae43687dd5f26e: <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.13-2Sam.8.15">2Sa 8:13-15</reference> “And David made (himself) a name, when he returned from smiting (i.e., from the defeat of) Aram, (and smote Edom) in the valley of Salt, eighteen thousand men.” The words enclosed in brackets are wanting in the Masoretic text as it has come down to us, and must have fallen out from a mistake of the copyist, whose eye strayed from את־ארם to את־אדום; for though the text is not “utterly unintelligible” without these words, since the passage might be rendered “after he had smitten Aram in the valley of Salt eighteen thousand men,” yet this would be decidedly incorrect, as the Aramaeans were not smitten in the valley of Salt, but partly at Medeba (<reference osisRef="1Chr.19.7">1Ch 19:7</reference>) and Helam (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.17">2Sa 10:17</reference>), and partly in their own land, which was very far away from the Salt valley. Moreover, the difficulty presented by the text cannot be removed, as <hi type="italic">Movers</hi> supposes, by changing את־ארם (Syria) into את־אדום (Edom), as the expression בּשׁבו (“when he returned”) would still be unexplained. The facts were probably these: Whilst David, or rather Israel, was entangled in the war with the Ammonites and Aramaeans, the Edomites seized upon the opportunity, which appeared to them a very favourable one, to invade the land of Israel, and advanced as far as the southern extremity of the Dead Sea. As soon, therefore, as the Aramaeans were defeated and subjugated, and the Israelitish army had returned from this war, David ordered it to march against the Edomites, and defeated them in the valley of Salt. This valley cannot have been any other than the Ghor adjoining the Salt mountain on the south of the Dead Sea, which really separates the ancient territories of Judah and Edom (<hi type="italic">Robinson</hi>, Pal. ii. 483). There Amaziah also smote the Edomites at a later period (2Ki 14:7). We gather more concerning this war of David from the text of the Chronicles (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.12">2Sa 8:12</reference>) taken in connection with 1Ki 11:15-16, and Psa 60:2. According to the Chronicles, it was Abishai the son of Zeruiah who smote the Edomites. This agrees very well not only with the account in 2Sa 10:10., to the effect that Abishai commanded a company in the war with the Syrians and Ammonites under the generalship of his brother Joab, but also with the heading to <reference osisRef="Ps.60.1-Ps.60.12">Psa 60:1-12</reference>, in which it is stated that Joab returned after the defeat of Aram, and smote the Edomites in the valley of Salt, twelve thousand men; and with 1Ki 11:15-16, in which we read that when David was in Edom, Joab, the captain of the host, came up to bury the slain, and smote every male in Edom, and remained six months in Edom with all Israel, till he had cut off every male in Edom. From this casual but yet elaborate notice, we learn that the war with the Edomites was a very obstinate one, and was not terminated all at once. The difference as to the number slain, which is stated to have been 18,000 in the text before us and in the Chronicles, and 12,000 in the heading to <reference osisRef="Ps.60.1-Ps.60.12">Psa 60:1-12</reference>, may be explained in a very simple manner, on the supposition that the reckonings made were only approximative, and yielded different results;<note placement="foot">Michaelis adduces a case in point from the Seven Years’ War. After the battle of Lissa, eight or twelve thousand men were reported to have been taken prisoners; but when they were all counted, including those who fell into the hands of the conquerors on the second, third, and fourth days of the flight, the number amounted to 22,000.</note> and the fact that David is named as the victor in the verse before us, Joab in <reference osisRef="Ps.60.1-Ps.60.12">Psa 60:1-12</reference>, and Abishai in the Chronicles, admits of a very easy explanation after what has just been observed. The Chronicles contain the most literal account. Abishai smote the Edomites as commander of the men engaged, Joab as commander-in-chief of the whole army, and David as king and supreme governor, of whom the writer of the Chronicles affirms, “The Lord helped David in all his undertakings.” After the defeat of the Edomites, David placed garrisons in the land, and made all Edom subject to himself. <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.15">2Sa 8:15</reference>-18. David’s Ministers. - To the account of David’s wars and victories there is appended a list of his official attendants, which is introduced with a general remark as to the spirit of his government. As king over all Israel, David continued to execute right and justice.
entries.49bd0764df5fe8522f21d3d0c50943f634537d86: <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.16">2Sa 8:16</reference> <div eID="gen4344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4345" type="x-p"/> The chief ministers were the following: - Joab (see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.18">2Sa 2:18</reference>) was “over the army,” i.e., commander-in-chief. Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud, of whom nothing further is known, was <hi type="italic">mazcir</hi>, chancellor; not merely the national annalist, according to the Septuagint and Vulgate (ἐπὶ τῶν ὑπομνημάτην, ὑπομνηματόγραφος; a <hi type="italic">commentariis</hi>), i.e., the recorder of the most important incidents and affairs of the nation, but an officer resembling the <hi type="italic">magister memoriae</hi> of the later Romans, or the waka nuvis of the Persian court, who keeps a record of everything that takes place around the king, furnishes him with an account of all that occurs in the kingdom, places his visé upon all the king’s commands, and keeps a special protocol of all these things (vid., Chardin, Voyages v. p. 258, and Paulsen, Regierung der Morgenländer, pp. 279-80).
entries.3adda7b9c9f15a361b225e2687cdcf5ee93101cb: <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.17">2Sa 8:17</reference> <div eID="gen4345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4346" type="x-p"/> Zadok the son of Ahitub, of the line of Eleazar (<reference osisRef="1Chr.6.8">1Ch 6:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.11-1Chr.6.12">1Ch 6:11-12</reference>), and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar, were cohanim, i.e., officiating high priests; the former at the tabernacle at Gibeon (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.39">1Ch 16:39</reference>), the latter probably at the ark of the covenant upon Mount Zion. Instead of Ahimelech, the Chronicles have Abimelech, evidently through a copyist’s error, as the name is written Ahimelech in <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.3">1Ch 24:3</reference>, 1Ch 24:6. But the expression “Ahimelech the son of Abiathar” is apparently a very strange one, as Abiathar was a son of Ahimelech according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.20">1Sa 22:20</reference>, and in other passages Zadok and Abiathar are mentioned as the two high priests in the time of David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.24">2Sa 15:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.35">2Sa 15:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.15">2Sa 17:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.12">2Sa 19:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.25">2Sa 20:25</reference>). This difference cannot be set aside, as Movers, Thenius, Ewald, and other suppose, by transposing the names, so as to read Abiathar the son of Ahimelech; for such a solution is precluded by the fact that, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.3">1Ch 24:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.6">1Ch 24:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.31">1Ch 24:31</reference>, Ahimelech is mentioned along with Zadok as head of the priests of the line of Ithamar, and according to <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.6">1Ch 24:6</reference> he was the son of Abiathar. It would therefore be necessary to change the name Ahimelech into Abiathar in this instance also, both in <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.3">1Ch 24:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.6">1Ch 24:6</reference>, and in the latter to transpose the two names. But there is not the slightest probability in the supposition that the names have been changed in so many passa<hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> We are therefore disposed to adopt the view held by Bertheau and Oehler, viz., that Abiathar the high priest, the son of Ahimelech, had also a son named Ahimelech, as it is by no means a rare occurrence for grandfather and grandson to have the same names (vid., <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.4-1Chr.6.15">1Ch 6:4-15</reference>), and also that this (the younger) Ahimelech performed the duties of high priest in connection with his father, who was still living at the commencement of Solomon’s reign (1Ki 2:27), and is mentioned in this capacity, along with Zadok, both here and in the book of Chronicles, possibly because Abiathar was ill, or for some other reason that we cannot discover. As Abiathar was thirty or thirty-five years old at the time when his father was put to death by Saul, according to what has already been observed at <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.3">1Sa 14:3</reference>, and forty years old at the death of Saul, he was at least forty-eight years old at the time when David removed his residence to Mount Zion, and might have had a son of twenty-five years of age, namely the Ahimelech mentioned here, who could have taken his father’s place in the performance of the functions of high priest when he was prevented by illness or other causes. The appearance of a son of Abiathar named Jonathan in <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.27">2Sa 15:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.17">2Sa 17:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.20">2Sa 17:20</reference>, is no valid argument against this solution of the apparent discrepancy; for, according to these passages, he was still very young, and may therefore have been a younger brother of Ahimelech. The omission of any allusion to Ahimelech in connection with Abiathar’s conspiracy with Adonijah against Solomon (1Ki 1:42-43), and the reference to his son Jonathan alone, might be explained on the supposition that Ahimelech had already died. But as there is no reference to Jonathan at the time when his father was deposed, no stress is to be laid upon the omission of any reference to Ahimelech. Moreover, when Abiathar was deposed after Solomon had ascended the throne, he must have been about eighty years of age. <hi type="italic">Seraiah</hi> was a scribe. Instead of <hi type="italic">Seraiah</hi>, we have <hi type="italic">Shavsha</hi> in the corresponding text of the Chronicles, and <hi type="italic">Sheva</hi> in the parallel passage 2Sa 20:25. Whether the last name is merely a mistake for Shavsha, occasioned by the dropping of שׁ, or an abbreviated form of Shisha and Shavsha, cannot be decided. <hi type="italic">Shavsha</hi> is not a copyist’s error, for in 1Ki 4:3 the same man is unquestionably mentioned again under the name of Shisha, who is called Shavsha in the Chronicles, <hi type="italic">Sheva</hi> (שׁיא) in the text of <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.25">2Sa 20:25</reference>, and here Seraiah. <hi type="italic">Seraiah</hi> also is hardly a copyist’s error, but another form for Shavsha or Shisha. The <hi type="italic">scribe</hi> was a secretary of state; not a military officer, whose duty it was to raise and muster the troops, for the technical expression for mustering the people was not ספר, but פּקד (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.2">2Sa 24:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.4">2Sa 24:4</reference>,<reference osisRef="2Sam.24.9">2Sa 24:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.5-1Chr.21.6">1Ch 21:5-6</reference>, etc.).
entries.c8afe2dea3c89d9a31283c2213657f3347be3a2b: <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.18">2Sa 8:18</reference> <hi type="italic">Benaiah</hi> the son of Jehoiada, a very brave hero of Kabzeel (see at 2Sa 23:20.), was over the <hi type="italic">Crethi</hi> and <hi type="italic">Plethi</hi>. Instead of והכּרתי, which gives no sense, and must be connected in some way with 1Ki 1:38, 1Ki 1:44, we must read הכּרתי על according to the parallel passage <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.23">2Sa 20:23</reference>, and the corresponding text of the Chronicles. The <hi type="italic">Crethi</hi> and <hi type="italic">Plethi</hi> were the king’s body-guard, σωματοφύλακες (Josephus, <hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. vii. 5, 4). The words are adjectives in form, but with a substantive meaning, and were used to indicate a certain rank, <hi type="italic">lit</hi>. the executioners and runners, like השּׁלישׁי   (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.8">2Sa 23:8</reference>). כּרתי, from כּרת, to cut down or exterminate, signifies <hi type="italic">confessor</hi>, because among the Israelites (see at 1Ki 2:25), as in fact throughout the East generally, the royal halberdiers had to execute the sentence of death upon criminals. פּלתי, from פלת (to fly, or be swift), is related to פּלט, and signifies <hi type="italic">runners</hi>. It is equivalent to רץ, a courier, as one portion of the halberdiers, like the ἄγγαροι of the Persians, had to convey the king’s orders to distant places (vid., <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.6">2Ch 30:6</reference>). This explanation is confirmed by the fact that the epithet והרצים הכּדי was afterwards applied to the king’s body-guard (2Ki 11:4, 2Ki 11:19), and that הכּרי for הכּרתי occurs as early as 2Sa 20:23. כּרי, from כוּר, <hi type="italic">fodit, perfodit,</hi> is used in the same sense.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi> (<hi type="italic">Thes. s. vv.</hi>) and Thenius (on 1Ki 1:38) both adopt this explanation; but the majority of the modern theologians decide in favour of Lakemacher’s opinion, to which <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> has given currency, viz., that the <hi type="italic">Crethi</hi> or <hi type="italic">Cari</hi> are Cretes or Carians, and the <hi type="italic">Pelethi</hi> Philistines (vid., <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, <hi type="italic">Krit</hi>. <hi type="italic">Gramm</hi>. p. 297, and <hi type="italic">Gesch. des Volkes Israel</hi>, pp. 330ff.; Bertheau, <hi type="italic">zur Geschichte Israel</hi>, p. 197; <hi type="italic">Movers</hi>, <hi type="italic">Phönizier</hi> i. p. 19). This view is chiefly founded upon the fact that the Philistines are called <hi type="italic">C'rethi</hi> in <reference osisRef="1Sam.30.14">1Sa 30:14</reference>, and <hi type="italic">C'rethim</hi> in Zep 2:5 and Eze 25:16. But in both the passages from the prophets the name is used with special reference to the meaning of the word הכרית, viz., to exterminate, cut off, as <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> has shown in the case of Ezekiel by adopting the rendering <hi type="italic">interficiam interfectores</hi> (I will slay the slayers) for את־כּרתים הכרתּי. The same play upon the words takes place in Zephaniah, upon which Strauss has correctly observed: “Zephaniah shows that this violence of theirs had not been forgotten, calling the Philistines <hi type="italic">Crethim</hi> for that very reason, <hi type="italic">ut sit nomen et omen</hi>.” Besides, in both these passages the true name <hi type="italic">Philistines</hi> stands by the side as well, so that the prophets might have used the name <hi type="italic">Crethim</hi> (slayers, exterminators) without thinking at all of 1Sa 30:14. In this passage it is true the name <hi type="italic">Crethi</hi> is applied to a branch of the Philistine people that had settled on the south-west of Philistia, and not to the Philistines generally. The idea that the name of a portion of the royal body-guard was derived from the Cretans is precluded, first of all, by the fact of its combination with הפּלתי (the Pelethites); for it is a totally groundless assumption that this name signifies the <hi type="italic">Philistines</hi>, and is a corruption of פלשׁתּים. There are no such contractions as these to be found in the Semitic languages, as <hi type="italic">Gesenius</hi> observes in his <hi type="italic">Thesaurus</hi> (<hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>), “<hi type="italic">quis hujusmodi contractionem in linguis Semiticis ferat?</hi>” <hi type="italic">Secondly</hi>, it is also precluded by the strangeness of such a combination of two synonymous names to denote the royal body-guard. “Who could believe it possible that two synonymous epithets should be joined together in this manner, which would be equivalent to saying Englishmen and Britons?” (<hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 1107). <hi type="italic">Thirdly</hi>, it is opposed to the title afterwards given to the body-guard, והרצים הכּרי   (2Ki 11:4, 2Ki 11:19), in which the <hi type="italic">Cari</hi> correspond to the <hi type="italic">Crethi</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.20.23">2Sa 20:23</reference>, and <hi type="italic">ha-razim</hi> to the <hi type="italic">Pelethi</hi>; so that the term <hi type="italic">pelethi</hi> can no more signify a particular tribe than the term razim can. Moreover, there are other grave objections to this interpretation. In the first place, the hypothesis that the Philistines were emigrants from Crete is merely founded upon the very indefinite statements of Tacitus (<hi type="italic">Hist</hi>. v. 3, 2), “<hi type="italic">Judaeos Creta insula profugos novissima Libyae insedisse memorant</hi>,” and that of Steph. Byz. (<hi type="italic">s. v.</hi> Γαζά), to the effect that the city of Gaza was once called <hi type="italic">Minoa</hi>, from <hi type="italic">Minos</hi> a king of Crete, - statements which, according to the correct estimate of Strauss (<hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>), “have all so evidently the marks of fables that they hardly merit discussion,” at all events when opposed to the historical testimony of the Old Testament (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.23">Deu 2:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.7">Amo 9:7</reference>), to the effect that the Philistines sprang from <hi type="italic">Caphtor</hi>. And secondly, “it is <hi type="italic">a priori</hi> altogether improbable, that a man with so patriotic a heart, and so devoted to the worship of the one God, should have surrounded himself with a <hi type="italic">foreign</hi> and <hi type="italic">heathen</hi> body-guard” (Thenius). This argument cannot be invalidated by the remark “that it is well known that at all times kings and princes have preferred to commit the protection of their persons to foreign mercenaries, having, as they thought, all the surer pledge of their devotedness in the fact that they did not spring from the nation, and were dependent upon the ruler alone” (Hitzig). For, in the first place, the expression “at all times” is one that must be very greatly modified; and secondly, this was only done by kings who did not feel safe in the presence of their own people, which was not the case with David. And the Philistines, those arch-foes of Israel, would have been the last nation that David would have gone to for the purpose of selecting his own body-guard. It is true that he himself had met with a hospitable reception in the land of the Philistines; but it must be borne in mind that it was not as king of Israel that he found refuge there, but as an outlaw flying from Saul the king of Israel, and even then the chiefs of the Philistines would not trust him (1Sa 29:3.). And when Hitzig appeals still further to the fact, that according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.2">2Sa 18:2</reference>, David handed over the command of a third of his army to a foreigner who had recently entered his service, having emigrated from Gath with a company of his fellow-countrymen (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.19-2Sam.15.20">2Sa 15:19-20</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.22">2Sa 15:22</reference>), and who had displayed the greatest attachment to the person of David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.21">2Sa 15:21</reference>), it is hardly necessary to observe that the fact of David’s welcoming a brave soldier into his army, when he had come over to Israel, and placing him over a division of the army, after he had proved his fidelity so decidedly as Ittai had at the time of Absalom’s rebellion, is no proof that he chose his body-guard from the Philistines. Nor can <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.18">2Sa 15:18</reference> be adduced in support of this, as the notion that, according to that passage, David had 600 Gathites in his service as body-guard, is simply founded upon a misinterpretation of the passage mentioned.</note> <div eID="gen4346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4347" type="x-p"/> And David’s sons were כּהנים (“confidants”); not priests, domestic priests, court chaplains, or spiritual advisers, as Gesenius, De Wette, and others maintain, but, as the title is explained in the corresponding text of the Chronicles, when the title had become obsolete, “the first at the hand (or side) of the king.” The correctness of this explanation is placed beyond the reach of doubt by 1Ki 4:5, where the cohen is called, by way of explanation, “the king’s friend.” The title <hi type="italic">cohen</hi> may be explained from the primary signification of the verb כּהן, as shown in the corresponding verb and noun in Arabic (“<hi type="italic">res alicujus gerere</hi>,” and “<hi type="italic">administrator alieni negotii</hi>”). These <hi type="italic">cohanim</hi>, therefore, were the king’s confidential advisers.  <chapter eID="2Sam.8"/> <div eID="gen4347" type="x-p"/>
